malinger

muh-LING-ger · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To malinger is to pretend to be ill in order to avoid work or duty.

The coach suspected the star player was malingering to skip the exhausting two-a-day practices.

Example

The private was accused of malingering, reporting a mysterious back pain each time his unit was due for a hard march.

Pain that mysteriously appears only before a hard march is exactly malingering.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shirk: To shirk is to dodge a duty you were given — by any means at all: hiding, dawdling, quietly leaving the work to others. Malinger names one specific method of dodging it: inventing an illness and using it as the excuse.

pretend to be sick: Anyone can pretend to be sick, for any reason — to win sympathy, to duck a party, to get attention. Malinger is narrower and more damning: the faked illness is aimed specifically at escaping work or duty, and it usually keeps happening.

slack: To slack is to stay at your post but barely work — slow, careless, minimal effort. There is no lie in it, and the task still limps along. Someone who malingers escapes the task completely, hiding behind an invented illness.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

volunteer: willingly offer to do a duty

Where it sits · how far one dodges duty

skip → malinger → desert

skip vs. malinger: Skip simply means missing something, a plain everyday word; malinger specifically means faking illness as the excuse for missing it.

desert vs. malinger: Desert (in a military sense) means abandoning a duty entirely and often permanently, while malinger is a smaller, ongoing deception -- staying present but dodging specific tasks.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — mal-: bad, badly (French/Latin)

root — inger: weak, sickly (uncertain further origin) (French (malingre))

Put it together: Malinger comes from French malingre, 'sickly,' built on mal- ('bad'). The exact root behind the rest of the word is debated, but the mal- ('bad') piece is clear and productive.

Where This Word Comes From: The sergeant wrote one word - malingerer - beside the private's name on the duty roster and underlined it twice.

Word Building

Malinger is almost always used for faking illness or injury specifically to escape work, military duty, or an unwanted task.
